id: I Too Have Been to Candyland

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I TOO have been to Candyland, but I found myself missing the death cult. I missed the spectacle of the wounded bones being opened and instrumented. Bill Varner, when he was still just a boy, wrote a stunning line of Arabic verse. He wrote: “The crescent moon is a scimitar; the sun, a severed head.” ¡Gran cantar! and this, when he still had to keep his books in a locker! And he’d never even held hands with a girl—God! Penn State in the 1980s! In those days, we all sat at the feet of a pig poet, deaf in one ear. One of these Dreadful “white-haired lovers”—oh, but he knew how to touch fire to fuse! That little stick of fire apt to launch a poetic career! But what is it now? Merely a billowing cloud of humidity floating out of a tree. Every turtle, snake, and bird is “born again”—oh, isn’t that so? The first time, Out the fêted cloaca—and the next, through the top of the shell. The “I” is Greek, the “it” Italian, and Dickinson is our Ghalib. But that Ridiculous piece of dirt you’re kissing on can never be anything but. Shut your eyes to what a worm he is, concentrate on his caress—but know Every half-truth is bound to call up its suppressed synoptic double. Close your eyes and moan softly, your head full of packed cotton—but know Every hidden camera’s cockpit must one day be delivered of its black box.

Keywords: TOO, Candyland, Bill

outputs.L1:
I too have been to Candyland, yet found myself longing for the death cult—missing the spectacle of wounded bones pried open and instrumented. Bill Varner, when he was still just a boy, composed a stunning line of Arabic verse: "The crescent moon is a scimitar; the sun, a severed head." ¡Gran cantar!—and this from a boy who still kept his books in a locker, who had never even held a girl's hand. God, Penn State in the 1980s! In those days we all sat at the feet of a pig poet, deaf in one ear—one of those dreadful "white-haired lovers." But he knew how to touch fire to fuse, how to strike that small flame capable of igniting a poetic career. And what remains of it now? Only a billowing cloud of humidity drifting out of a tree.

Every turtle, snake, and bird is "born again"—isn't that so? The first time, expelled from the fêted cloaca; the next, breaking through the crown of the shell. The "I" is Greek, the "it" Italian, and Dickinson is our Ghalib. Yet that ridiculous clod of earth you're kissing can never be more than what it is. Shut your eyes to the worm he truly is; lose yourself in his caress—but know that every half-truth summons forth its suppressed and synoptic double. Close your eyes and moan softly, your head packed full of cotton—but know that every hidden camera's cockpit must, in time, surrender its black box.
outputs.L2: I've also visited Candyland, yet found myself yearning for the death cult instead. What I longed for was the sight of shattered bones being pried open and probed. Bill Varner, back when he was merely a child, composed an extraordinary line of Arabic poetry: "The crescent moon serves as a scimitar; the sun becomes a decapitated head." What a magnificent song! And this from someone who still stored his textbooks in a school locker! He hadn't even experienced holding a girl's hand—imagine that! Penn State, back in the eighties! During that era, we gathered around a swine-like poet who'd lost hearing in one ear. This dreadful figure, one among the "silver-haired romantics"—yet he possessed the gift of igniting sparks into flame! That small flame capable of igniting an entire poetic destiny! But what remains of it today? Nothing but a swelling mist of moisture drifting from tree branches. Every turtle, every serpent, every bird experiences rebirth—isn't that remarkable? First emerging through the celebrated cloaca, then later breaking free through the shell's crown. The self springs from Greek origins, the object from Italian ones, while Dickinson stands as our equivalent to Ghalib. Yet that absurd clump of earth you're pressing your lips against will forever remain exactly that. Close your eyes to his wormlike nature and focus instead on his tenderness—understand, though, that every partial truth inevitably summons forth its hidden, comprehensive counterpart. Shut your eyes and release a gentle sigh, your mind stuffed like cotton wadding—but recognize that every concealed surveillance device must eventually surrender its recorded evidence.
outputs.L3:
# Return to Candyland

I find myself back in Candyland again—that saccharine geography of easy comfort, where every square promises advancement without cost, every color-coded path leads gently toward a predetermined finish. And yet, perversely, I ache for the death cult. I miss its theater, its unflinching gaze into consequence. I miss the graphic imagery of wounded bones laid bare on examination tables, the forensic tenderness with which fracture and marrow were once observed, named, understood. There was a rigor to that darkness that Candyland's pastel innocence cannot replicate. The death cult demanded witness; Candyland only demands participation.

This longing pulls me backward, inevitably, to Bill Varner—a name that still carries the static charge of adolescent genius. He was a prodigy in the truest, most unsettling sense: a boy who had not yet lived enough to earn his metaphors, and yet wrote them anyway, fully formed, terrifying in their maturity. I remember lines of his rendered in Arabic verse, where he compared the crescent moon to a scimitar—curved, patient, waiting to be drawn—and the sun to a severed head, blazing and terrible, hoisted above the horizon like a trophy of some cosmic violence. He wrote this with the untroubled confidence of youth, innocent of the darkness he so precisely conjured, inexperienced in everything except language itself.

It was at Penn State, in the 1980s, that I first understood what it meant to be near such fire without being consumed by it—or perhaps I was consumed, slowly, in ways I'm still discovering. Those years hold the shape of formation for me, and at their center stands a figure I can only call, with equal parts affection and discomfort, the pig poet: a mentor as flawed as he was magnetic, animalistic in his appetites and unfiltered in his speech, and yet somehow the very source from which my creative hunger first sprang. I revered him not despite his crudeness but perhaps because of it—he taught me that poetry did not require purity, only intensity. He ignited something in me that has never fully gone out, though I have spent decades trying to understand whether what he lit was a flame or a fuse.

There is, I think, a mythic logic to all of this—the way certain creatures are said to be born twice: the turtle cracking free of its shell only to emerge fully into a harder world, the snake shedding its old skin to reveal an identical, renewed self beneath, the bird breaking first from the egg and then, metaphorically, from the nest into flight. I feel this doubling in my own literary identity, this sense of having been born once into language and again into meaning. I think of Dickinson, coiled and precise, writing her small ferocious hymns to mortality; I think of Ghalib, mourning and reveling in the same breath, his couplets thick with the ache of unrequited everything. Between them—the American recluse and the Urdu master—I locate something of my own splintered inheritance, a poetic self assembled from disparate rebirths, none of them complete, all of them necessary.

But I want to close with a caution, one I have earned through repetition and heartbreak: illusions do not last. Whether romantic or ideological, the comforting deceptions we construct—the Candylands we build to protect ourselves from the death cult's honesty—will eventually collapse. Beneath every performed self lies a suppressed double, waiting. Beneath every carefully managed narrative sits a hidden camera, its black box recording what we tried so hard not to show. Truth accumulates in the dark, patient as Varner's scimitar moon, inevitable as his severed-head sun rising. We may delay the reckoning, but we cannot indefinitely avoid it. Sooner or later, the tape plays back.
outputs.L4:
# Fragments of Memory and Metaphor

There was a boy once, at Penn State, whose mind burned brighter than the autumn leaves scattering across the quad. He spoke in verses before he understood what verses meant—words tumbling from him like water finding its inevitable path downhill. Professors would pause mid-lecture when he raised his hand, not because he demanded attention, but because he seemed to pull truths from some hidden reservoir none of them could locate. That was decades ago now, or perhaps it was yesterday. Time folds strangely when you're chasing the ghost of who you used to be.

The maple trees knew something we didn't. Every autumn, they performed their small deaths with such theatrical grace—crimson, gold, the slow surrender of chlorophyll—only to insist, months later, on being born again. Nature never apologizes for this cycle, never explains why destruction must precede renewal. It simply *is*, the way Dickinson understood the slant of light on winter afternoons, the way she wrote of hope as "the thing with feathers" while death perched on her other shoulder, patient, unhurried.

I think of Ghalib sometimes, his couplets thick with longing and contradiction—*hazaron khwahishen aisi*, a thousand desires, each one worth dying for, and yet none of them satisfied. He understood something about the architecture of want: that desire builds cathedrals in the mind that reality can never quite house. The poet at Penn State understood this too, though he wouldn't have called it that. He called it hunger. He called it the ache of almost-arriving.

There's a particular quality to memory that resembles moonlight on water—you can see the shape of something true, but touch it and it scatters into a thousand refracted pieces. Was the boy truly brilliant, or did we need him to be, in that particular season of our lives when we were all reaching for something to believe in? The mind constructs its mythologies carefully, brick by brick, until we can no longer distinguish the foundation from the ornament.

This is the nature of every comfortable lie we tell ourselves. We paint over the water stains rather than fixing the leak. We say "everything is fine" while the foundation cracks beneath our feet, widening in the dark where we cannot see it, cannot measure its slow betrayal. The half-truth is architecturally unstable by design—it must be, because truth is not a decoration you can simply choose to omit. It is structural. It bears weight whether we acknowledge it or not.

Consider the way autumn always arrives, uninvited, dismantling summer's pleasant fiction that warmth is permanent. Consider how winter strips the trees bare, revealing the stark geometry beneath the leaves' seasonal deception—the architecture that was always there, waiting. This is not cruelty. This is simply how the world insists on honesty, eventually, regardless of our preferences.

Ghalib knew this too, in his way—that longing itself is often a beautiful lie we tell ourselves about the nature of fulfillment, a comfortable narrative that keeps us moving toward horizons that recede as we approach them. And yet the ache is real, the mind's stubborn architecture of hope. The lie and the truth exist in the same breath, the same line of verse.

Perhaps this is what the young poet at Penn State understood, in the frost-touched clarity of youth: that every comfortable half-truth we construct—about brilliance, about permanence, about the durability of any given season—carries within it the seed of its own unraveling. The suppressed reality does not vanish simply because we refuse to look at it. It waits. It accumulates pressure in the dark spaces we've chosen not to illuminate.

And then, in its own time, indifferent to our readiness, it surfaces—the way spring insists on arriving after the harshest winter, the way truth insists on emerging from beneath even our most carefully constructed illusions. Not as punishment, but as inevitability. The nature of things. The quiet, persistent grammar of the real, asserting itself against the fictions we have grown so comfortably accustomed to believing.
outputs.L5:
# A Game of Candyland

Bill had not played Candyland in over twenty years, not since his own children were small enough to believe that a path made of gumdrops could lead somewhere magical. So when his granddaughter Emma pulled the worn box from the closet, blowing a thin layer of dust off the lid, Bill felt a strange mixture of nostalgia and reluctance.

"Grandpa, you have to play too!" she insisted, her eyes wide with the kind of enthusiasm only a six-year-old could muster for a board game older than her parents.

Bill smiled and lowered himself into the small plastic chair, his knees protesting the whole way down. The board unfolded between them, its colors as vivid as he remembered—the Peppermint Forest, the Lollipop Woods, the treacherous Molasses Swamp that had ended so many childhood games in tears.

"Alright," he said, picking up the tiny gingerbread man that served as his token. "But I should warn you, I used to be very good at this."

Emma giggled. "It's not really a skill game, Grandpa. It's just luck."

She was right, of course. Candyland requires no strategy, no clever maneuvering—just the turn of a card and the willingness to move forward, wherever the path leads. Bill drew a card and moved his piece three spaces to a purple square.

As they played, he found himself thinking about how life itself was often like this simple game. You don't always choose your path. Sometimes you land on a shortcut that carries you forward unexpectedly; other times you're stuck, waiting for the right card to free you. Too many people spent their lives trying to control every outcome, when really, all that mattered was staying in the game.

Emma drew the dreaded Lord Licorice card and groaned dramatically, sliding her piece back to the start. "This is so unfair!"

"That's the game," Bill said, chuckling. "Some days are like that. You just draw again."

By the time Emma's piece reached the Candy Castle, declaring her the winner, Bill realized he'd genuinely enjoyed himself—more than he expected, more than felt reasonable for a man his age playing a children's game on a Tuesday afternoon. But maybe that was the point. Joy doesn't require justification. It doesn't need to be earned through complexity or effort.

"Can we play again?" Emma asked, already gathering the cards.

"Of course," Bill said, settling back into the little chair. "But this time, I call the gingerbread man again. For old times' sake."

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem that mixes personal nostalgia about a 1980s college poetry workshop with surreal, aphoristic imagery about nature, myth, and hidden truths.
counterfactuals.output:
**Smoke Break, Wednesday Workshop, 1987**

The mimeograph fluid was its own drug, that purple ghost-smell rising off the pages Professor Halloran passed around like communion wafers, and we'd hold them to our faces before reading, inhaling the fresh violet chemical breath of somebody's villanelle about her grandmother's hands, and I think now that ink was the only honest thing in that room, bleeding through thin paper the way truth bleeds through whatever we build to hide it—

the radiator clanked its iambic pentameter against the wall, five beats, always five, and Deborah with the cigarette voice said *nature poems are just funerals we haven't admitted to yet*, and I wrote that down on my hand in blue pen because I didn't have paper, because the dead leave instructions everywhere if you're paying attention, in the veins of maple leaves, in the way a river forgets its own name a thousand times before reaching the sea—

the myth was always this: someone drowns, someone becomes a flower, someone's grief turns into an echo that outlives the throat that made it, and we sat in that circle of folding chairs believing we were the first to notice this, believing our twenty-year-old sorrows were original as Eden, and maybe they were, maybe every sorrow is original the way every snowflake is original before it melts into the same grey slush as all the others—

Tom Kilbride read a poem about his father's hands and someone cried and someone else said *the birds don't testify, they just witness*, and I didn't understand it then but I understand it now, folded into the coat closet of memory next to the smell of clove cigarettes and Nina's paisley skirt, next to the fact that all creeks are just the earth admitting it can't hold its own water, all forests are cathedrals built by things too patient to know they were building anything—

we were twenty and thought poems could save us, thought language was a rope thrown down a well, and maybe it is, maybe the well is just time and the rope is just attention, and somewhere Halloran is still saying *cut the abstraction, show me the thing*, and the thing was always this: a doe standing at the treeline at dusk, unbothered by our metaphors, just eating, just being the actual animal our poems could only gesture toward—

the myth again, always the myth: Orpheus looking back not from doubt but from love, because love always turns around, that's its whole function, its whole terrible architecture, and Eurydice dissolving into shadow not as punishment but as the truth of all beloveds, that they are smoke shaped like a person, that we build gods out of the missing—

and the hidden truth, the one none of us wrote down: that we were already becoming the ghosts we'd later write about, already the used-to-be, already fossils forming in the sediment of that basement room with its bad fluorescent light, its Styrofoam cups of bad coffee, its purple-inked pages passed hand to hand like something almost sacred, like something that might, if we were patient enough, quiet enough, actually save us from the ordinary weather of our dying—

the radiator still clanking, the snow outside still falling in its old unoriginal way, and somewhere in all that white, a truth was hiding the way truths always hide: in plain sight, in the shape of something else, in the leaf, the doe, the echo, the poem we didn't know yet we'd spend the rest our lives trying to finish.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental literary prose that name-drops a fictional poet named Bill Varner, references Ghalib and Dickinson, and ends with cryptic moral aphorisms.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Unwritten Letters

Bill Varner used to say that every poem is a suicide note written to someone who hasn't decided whether to die yet. I think about this in supermarkets, mostly, under the fluorescent hum that makes everyone look like they're already remembering themselves.

Ghalib knew something about the shop of the world being a child's toy—*mumkin hai*, he wrote, that a man might weep with joy at even this. Dickinson knew the slant of light on winter afternoons that oppresses like cathedral tunes. Between the two of them, an ocean and a century, but both circling the same drain: how to say the unsayable without drowning in the saying.

Varner's last collection—*Static and Psalm*, 1987, out of print, forgotten by everyone except me and possibly his ex-wife—contained a poem called "Instructions for My Funeral" that instructed nothing. Just a list of weather conditions. Rain probable. Wind from the northwest. A chance of the sun forgetting its one job.

I keep thinking the ghazal and the riddle-poem are cousins who never met at the family reunion. Both hoard their meanings like Depression-era grandmothers hoard rubber bands. Both know that directness is a kind of violence.

There is a version of this essay where I explain what any of this means. This is not that version.

What I know: Ghalib wrote about wine and ruin like they were the same intoxication. Dickinson wrote letters to the world that never wrote back, and called this correspondence anyway. Varner wrote about static like it was a form of prayer—the in-between channel, the frequency that belongs to no station, the sound of God clearing his throat before deciding not to speak.

*

Here, then, cryptically, as promised:

The bird that sings loudest has already been eaten.

Forgiveness is a debt paid in a currency that doesn't exist yet.

What you inherit, you must first pretend to have chosen.

The mirror lies only about which direction time is moving.

To love completely is to become slightly illegible to yourself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, allusive monologue in the voice of a jaded former poetry student reminiscing about a charismatic mentor, weaving in animal symbolism and Cold War-era paranoia imagery like "hidden cameras" and "black boxes."
counterfactuals.output:
You know, I still can't drink coffee without thinking of him — the way he'd hold the cup like it was a small bird he'd caught and didn't want to kill, didn't want to let go either. That was the thing about Professor Vantage: everything in his hands became evidence. A pencil. A stanza. Your face, when you'd failed to see the metaphor he'd already mapped out in his head like a defector's exfil route.

He taught us that poetry was surveillance conducted lovingly. That every image was a hidden camera planted in the architecture of feeling, recording what we were too cowardly to say straight out. "Line breaks," he'd say, "are where the wire taps in." We nodded like fools in a bread line, starving for whatever he'd hand out that week — Akhmatova smuggled in a coat lining, Celan's black milk poured out like static from a jammed radio frequency.

He loved animals as metaphor the way spies love dead drops — something to hold the meaning until it could be retrieved by the right reader. The fox that means cunning and hunger both. The owl that means wisdom until you realize it's just very good at not being seen, at rotating its head while the rest of the world thinks it's still facing forward. He said, "A wolf in a poem is never just a wolf. It's a black box, recording the crash before it happens."

I think now — bitterly, the way you love someone bitterly after they've become myth instead of man — that he was always performing for cameras only he could see. He talked about workshops like debriefings. He'd say revision was "erasing your fingerprints from the file." He made us paranoid in the best way, the way Cold War children were paranoid, checking under desks for devices, assuming every silence was a silence someone was profiting from.

Where is he now? Retired, they say, somewhere with better weather and worse liver. I picture him still, some agent gone to seed, still speaking in code to no one, still convinced the horses in Chagall and the sparrows in Bishop were ciphers passed between exiled hearts. Maybe they were. Maybe he was right and we were the compromised assets, bugged by our own desire to be seen clearly by someone who'd trained his whole life to see.

I don't write poems anymore. I check the locks twice, though. Old habits. Old handlers. He taught me that every silence has a listener, and I have never once, in the years since, felt unheard — only unrecorded, which somehow feels worse.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, associative text that blends confessional memory (Penn State, a "pig poet," first crushes) with mythic and religious imagery of rebirth, ending in two parallel gnomic warnings about truth and deception.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Pig Poet's Confession

I was seventeen at Penn State when I first understood
that swine could write sonnets better than boys who shaved.
He kept a notebook in the mud, that pig poet,
rooting out metaphors between the troughs and the football stadium's shadow.
His snout knew iambics. His curl-tail counted syllables.

I loved a girl named Something-like-morning
in a dormitory that smelled of instant coffee and Old Testament guilt.
She had the kind of hands that could split an atom
or a psalm, I couldn't tell which, I was seventeen,
I didn't know yet that all first loves are Lazarus—
they die and you weep and then somehow
they're standing in the doorway again
wrapped in the same white cloth, asking for soup.

The pig poet said: *rebirth is just recycling with better PR.*
He'd read too much Ezekiel, dry bones clacking
like typewriter keys in that valley,
and he believed—actually believed—
that if you oinked the right words in the right order
God would reassemble you from the disassembly line of your worst year.

I wanted to be reborn too. Everyone at that school did,
we walked around like church confetti,
shredded hymnals looking for a wind to lift us.

The girl—Something-like-morning—she left in October,
took the pig poet's notebook with her, the traitor,
said she was going to publish it under her own name in Rome
where the rebirth industry has better infrastructure,
older stones, more reliable resurrection scaffolding.

I stood in the quad. The pig poet oinked something in Latin.
I think it was an elegy. I think it was for me.

*

Here is what I know now, filtered through pig-Latin and stolen notebooks and a love that rose only to leave again:

**The truth will set you free, but first it will check your ID at the door and ask why you're really here.**

**A lie, well-told, can resurrect anything except itself—so tell it once, and mean it like a prayer you don't expect to be answered.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
the body remembers what the sentence forgets which is to say your mouth was a colon opening onto more mouth and I fell into you the way a reader falls into free indirect discourse never touching bottom never sure whose thought this is now yours now mine now the narrator's hand between your legs like a footnote nobody asked for

Candyland is what we called the apartment because everything in it wanted to kill us softly the sugar walls the peppermint sheets the way desire arranges itself into a board game where you move forward by being eaten

theory says the author is dead but you were so alive against the doorframe your spine writing itself into the wood grain a marginalia of want I could not stop annotating

every love is a death cult with a congregation of two we built our altar out of Tuesday afternoons and called it liturgy called it the body's only scripture the gospel according to your throat

there is a version of you and a version of you that is not you the synoptic double who shows up in dreams speaking the same words in a different tense as if memory itself required two witnesses to convict the past of ever having happened

the apocalypse will not arrive with trumpets it arrives already having arrived it arrives as the taste of you fading from a mouth that keeps talking anyway keeps performing hunger like liturgy like a text that footnotes its own disappearance

Roland Barthes said the text is a tissue of quotations and so were you a tissue a citation of every mouth before mine every death cult of two that dissolved into acronym into ash

Candyland burned we knew it would burn the whole time we were building it out of sugar and doorframes and the synoptic double kept writing us into two different endings

in one ending you survive
in the other you become theory
become the thing I cite instead of touch
become the death cult's last member
speaking in tongues about a body
that will not stop
almost arriving
